analysis.one_liner: Bans three classes of toxic pesticides and tightens EPA oversight of pesticide safety.
analysis.headline: Introduced in August 2020 with five cosponsors, the bill never received a committee hearing or vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would immediately cancel EPA registration of organophosphate pesticides, neonicotinoid pesticides, and paraquat, which the bill's findings link to brain damage in children, pollinator collapse, and Parkinson's disease. It would suspend any pesticide the European Union or Canada has banned, cap 'conditional' pesticide registrations at two years, require full disclosure of inert ingredients, let local governments set stricter pesticide rules than their states, and create mandatory reporting of farmworker poisonings with penalties for employers who fail to report. It died in the Senate Agriculture Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmworkers, who are disproportionately poisoned by pesticides, would gain mandatory incident reporting, bilingual labels, protection from retaliation, and up to $25,000 rewards for reporting unreported exposures. Children, whose scientists have linked organophosphate exposure to neurodevelopmental damage, and rural residents and consumers generally would be exposed to fewer toxic chemicals. Beekeepers and the food supply that depends on pollinators would benefit from the neonicotinoid ban.

how_it_helps.text: Immediately and permanently cancels registration of all organophosphate pesticides, all neonicotinoid pesticides, and paraquat, and prohibits sale of existing stocks [S3].
Requires the EPA to suspend any pesticide that the European Union or Canada has banned, rather than continuing to allow 72 pesticides the EU has banned or is phasing out [S3].
Lets any person petition the EPA to designate a pesticide as dangerous, with automatic suspension if the EPA misses its 90-day review deadline, and allows citizen lawsuits to enforce the law [S3].

Caps conditional pesticide registrations at two years and cancels outstanding conditional registrations not yet fulfilled, ending a practice the bill says covers roughly 65 percent of pesticide registrations [S3].
Requires pesticide labels to list all inert ingredients, which can make up 99 percent of a product and can include carcinogens, and to be printed in English and Spanish [S3].

Creates a mandatory farmworker incident reporting system with fines for employers who fail to report, criminal penalties for retaliation, and immediate suspension of any pesticide that kills a farmworker [S3].
Lets states and local governments enact pesticide restrictions stricter than federal rules, reversing state preemption that has blocked community protections [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers lose the registration and sale of three entire chemical classes and face tighter review, shorter conditional registrations, and mandatory disclosure of product contents. Farmers lose access to organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat as pest-control tools and would need substitutes, and agricultural employers face new reporting obligations and penalties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pesticide makers and growers using them

drawbacks.text: The bans take effect immediately by operation of law without individual safety review or any consideration of economic cost, so farmers lose these tools even where safer substitutes are not readily available, and crop yields or costs could suffer [S3].
Manufacturers lose existing inventory and must absorb cancellation without the notice-and-comment process that normally precedes cancellation of a registered pesticide [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health stakes are large: the bill's findings cite neurodevelopmental harm to children, Parkinson's disease from paraquat, and jeopardy to 97 percent of endangered species from organophosphates. But the design is blunt — class-wide bans with no case-by-case review and no weighing of agricultural costs could disrupt farming before substitutes are fully in place, and opponents would argue the EPA, not Congress, should decide pesticide-by-pesticide. The tradeoff is a genuine public-health gain against a real but transitionable cost to agriculture.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in August 2020, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Udall introduced the bill on August 4, 2020, joined by five cosponsors — four Democrats and one Independent [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote followed; the bill's action history ends with the committee referral, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers keep selling organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat, and growers keep using them; farmworkers and communities near treated fields gain nothing. Udall reintroduced the bill in the next Congress.

for.name: Tom Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat and tighten EPA pesticide review.

for.name: 5 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Warren, Booker, and Sanders named in the introduction [S1][S4].

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on August 4, 2020 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; with a Republican majority, bills not reported out of committee never reached the floor.

against.name: Pesticide manufacturers and agricultural industry groups
against.role: Industry stakeholders in organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed congressional bans on these pesticide classes, arguing farmers need them and the EPA review process should decide.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes, but the sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent, and the Republican-controlled Agriculture Committee took no action, leaving the bill stalled along a partisan shape.

industries.note: The bill permanently cancels registration for three chemical classes, blocks sale of existing stocks, and imposes disclosure, reporting, and review requirements that shrink the industry's market and raise its costs. Its interest in continuing sales runs against the public-health protections ordinary people would get.

Growers lose access to organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat as pest-control tools on short notice, which could raise costs or cut yields. They also gain from healthier pollinator populations and reduced exposure risks to their own workers and families.
Canceling neonicotinoids addresses the pollinator decline the bill's findings document, protecting honey production and the pollination services that fruit, vegetable, and nut growers depend on.

Employers must report every farmworker poisoning through a federal online system, face $1,000-per-day fines for failures and criminal penalties for retaliation, and lose pesticide registrations after serious incidents.
